title: Tokenisation, context windows, and why cost grows the way it does
story:
A model does not read characters and does not read words. It reads tokens: pieces produced by a scheme that splits text into units drawn from a fixed vocabulary, where common sequences become single units and rare ones get broken into several.

That arrangement is a compromise and each side of it explains a class of observed behaviour. Splitting on characters would give a tiny vocabulary and very long sequences. Splitting on words would give short sequences and a vocabulary that can never be complete, since new words keep arriving and every unknown one becomes unrepresentable. Subword pieces sit between: the vocabulary is bounded, anything can be represented as some sequence of pieces, and common text stays short.

Several things that look like defects follow directly. Text in a language underrepresented when the vocabulary was built fragments into many more pieces than equivalent text in a well-represented one, which means it costs more to process and consumes more of the available window for the same content. Arithmetic is unreliable partly because a number is split into pieces that do not correspond to digits, so the model is not seeing the structure the arithmetic depends on. Counting letters in a word is hard because the word may be a single token, and the letters are not individually present in what the model receives. None of these are reasoning failures; they are consequences of the input representation, and treating them as reasoning failures leads to the wrong fixes.

The window is the number of tokens the model can attend to at once, and it is a hard boundary rather than a performance consideration. Beyond it, content is not degraded — it is absent.

Now the cost, which is the part worth being precise about because two different growth rates get conflated.

The weights are read once per forward pass regardless of how long the sequence is, so that part of the cost is flat in sequence length. Attention is not: relating every position to every other position means the number of pairs grows with the square of the length. Double the sequence and the pairwise work quadruples.

So the cost of a request has a component that is roughly proportional to length and a component proportional to length squared, and which dominates depends on where you are. At short lengths the weights dominate and doubling the input roughly doubles the work. At long lengths the pairwise term dominates and doubling the input roughly quadruples it. That is why long-context pricing and latency feel disproportionate — not because anyone is being penalised, but because the quantity that grows fastest has taken over.

Two further cost facts that follow from the same structure. The keys and values for every position must be retained while generating, so memory grows with the length as well as time, and that memory is what limits how many requests can be served at once. And a long prompt is paid for at every generation step that attends over it, so a large context is not a one-time charge.

One thing worth stating because it is frequently assumed. A larger window is not the same as the model using it well. Being able to attend to a position and actually making good use of what is there are different properties, and the first is a specification while the second is an empirical question about a particular model. So a window figure tells you what cannot be done rather than what can.

problem.name: The input representation and its two growth rates
problem.shape: Text must be converted into units a model can process, and the length of the result drives the cost.
tell: a model miscounts letters or mishandles digits
the same content costs noticeably more in one language than another
latency or price grows faster than the input length
a long window is assumed to mean the whole window is used well
problem.move: Reason about length in tokens rather than characters or words, and separate the two cost terms: the weights are flat in length, the pairwise attention grows with its square. Then treat behaviour that depends on characters or digits as a representation problem rather than a reasoning one.
problem.invariant: Cost has a term roughly proportional to sequence length and a term proportional to its square, so which dominates depends on the length — doubling a short input roughly doubles the work and doubling a long one roughly quadruples it.
problem.breaks: A window size states what the model can attend to, not what it uses well. Being able to reach a position and making good use of what is there are different properties — the first is a specification, the second an empirical question about a particular model — so the figure bounds what is impossible rather than describing what works.

worked.reasoning:
Because the cost has two components with different growth rates, and which one dominates depends on the length you are already at.

problem.practice: Take a paragraph and the same content translated into another language you know, and compare the token counts your provider reports. The ratio is what that language costs per unit of meaning, and it is a property of the vocabulary rather than of the text.

beats.broke: Splitting text into characters gives very long sequences and splitting into words gives a vocabulary that can never be complete, since new words keep arriving and each unknown one is unrepresentable.
beats.fix: Use subword pieces from a fixed vocabulary, so the vocabulary is bounded, anything can be represented, and common text stays short — then reason about length in those units.
beats.cost: The pairwise attention term grows with the square of the length while the weights stay flat, so which dominates depends on where you are — and the retained keys and values make memory grow with length too.

takeaway: Cost has a term flat in length and a term growing with its square, so doubling a short input doubles the work and doubling a long one quadruples it — and the model's trouble with digits and letter-counting is the input representation rather than reasoning.
